Wording: two independent witnesses print this sentence as Fagles' 2006 rendering of Aeneid 1.203 and set it against the rival versions, which read quite differently (Dryden 1697 An hour will come, with pleasure to relate / Your sorrows past, as benefits of Fate; Williams 1910 It well may be / some happier hour will find this memory fair; Mandelbaum 1971 Perhaps one day you will remember even / these our adversities with pleasure; Fitzgerald 1983 Some day, perhaps, remembering even this / Will be a pleasure; Ahl 2007 Maybe the day'll come when even this will be joy to remember; Kline 2016 perhaps one day you'll even delight in remembering this). No drift: the shipped line is Fagles and no one else, and it is not a blend. Verse rule: both witnesses print the other translators' renderings broken with a slash and Fagles' as a single unbroken line, so this is one whole verse line of Fagles and there is no break to mark. Attribution and speaker: it is Aeneas, inside the O socii speech to his men on the Libyan shore after the storm, and the speaker is named in the source as the character trap requires. It is not the Virgil on the misattribution list, which is fortune favours the bold at 10.284 and belongs to Turnus. ONE CORRECTION TO THE EVIDENCE, NOT TO THE SHIPPED LINE: the evidence field calls 1.203 the close of Aeneas' speech. It is not. The speech runs 1.198 to 1.207 and four lines follow (per varios casus ... durate, et vosmet rebus servate secundis), so 203 falls midway through the exhortation. The source line makes no such claim and needs no change; only the evidence locator should drop the word closing.
